topics.title: 4.1.1 Energy changes in a system, and the ways energy is stored before and after such changes

outcomes.text: Define a system as an object or group of objects whose energy stores change when it changes.
Describe the changes in how energy is stored in common situations such as a thrown ball, a collision, a slowing vehicle or a kettle boiling.
Calculate the energy changes in a system from heating, work done by forces and work done by a current, and show how energy is redistributed on a common scale.
Calculate the energy of a moving object, a stretched spring and an object raised above the ground.
Recall and use kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed squared.
Apply elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x extension squared, within the limit of proportionality.
Recall and use gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x height.
Calculate the change in thermal energy using mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change.
State that specific heat capacity is the energy needed to warm 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree Celsius.
Required practical 1: investigate the specific heat capacity of materials by linking energy supplied to temperature rise.
Define power as the rate of energy transfer or of work done.
Recall and use power = energy transferred / time and power = work done / time.
State that 1 joule per second is 1 watt, and give examples comparing the power of two devices doing the same job.
State that energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated but never created or destroyed, giving closed-system examples.
Describe with examples how energy is dissipated into less useful stores and is often called wasted.
Explain ways to reduce unwanted energy transfers, such as lubrication and thermal insulation.
Explain that higher thermal conductivity gives a faster rate of energy transfer by conduction.
Describe how wall thickness and thermal conductivity affect a building's rate of cooling.
Required practical 2 (physics only): investigate how well different materials insulate and what affects insulation.
Calculate efficiency as useful output energy transfer divided by total input energy transfer.
Calculate efficiency using useful power output divided by total power input, as a decimal or percentage.
(Higher tier) Describe ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer.
Name the main energy resources: fossil fuels, nuclear, bio-fuel, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, tides, Sun and waves.
Distinguish renewable resources, which are replenished as used, from non-renewable ones.
Compare how resources are used for transport, electricity generation and heating.
Explain why some energy resources are more reliable than others.
Describe the environmental impact of using different energy resources.
Explain patterns and trends in the use of energy resources.
Discuss how science can identify environmental problems from energy use but political, social, ethical or economic factors limit solving them.
Use standard circuit symbols to draw and interpret circuit diagrams.
State that a source of potential difference is needed for charge to flow round a closed circuit.
Define current as the rate of flow of charge and use charge flow = current x time.
State that current has the same value everywhere in a single closed loop.
Explain that for a given potential difference, greater resistance gives smaller current.
Recall and use potential difference = current x resistance.
Required practical 3: build circuits to investigate factors affecting resistance, including wire length and resistors in series and parallel.
Explain that some resistors have constant resistance while others change as current changes.
State that an ohmic conductor at constant temperature has current directly proportional to potential difference.
State that the resistance of a filament lamp rises as its filament gets hotter.
Describe a diode as passing current one way only, with very high resistance in reverse.
State that a thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises and describe uses such as thermostats.
State that an LDR's resistance falls as light intensity rises and describe uses such as automatic lights.
Explain and draw a circuit to measure a component's resistance using current and potential difference readings.
Use graphs to decide whether circuit elements are linear or non-linear and relate the curves to their function.
Required practical 4: investigate I-V characteristics of a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor.
State the rules for series circuits: same current, shared potential difference, resistances add.
State the rules for parallel circuits: same potential difference, currents add, total resistance less than the smallest resistor.
Build and check series and parallel circuits using circuit diagrams.
Explain why adding resistors in series raises total resistance but adding them in parallel lowers it.
Explain the design and use of dc series circuits for measurement and testing.
Calculate currents, potential differences and resistances in dc series circuits using equivalent resistance.
State that UK mains is ac at 50 Hz and about 230 V.
Explain the difference between direct and alternating potential difference.
Describe the three-core cable and the colour coding of live, neutral and earth wires.
State the roles of the live, neutral and earth wires and their potentials relative to earth.
Explain why a live wire can be dangerous even with the switch open.
Explain the dangers of any connection between the live wire and earth.
Explain how a device's power relates to potential difference, current and energy change over time.
Recall and use power = potential difference x current and power = current squared x resistance.
Describe how appliances transfer energy from batteries or mains to motors' kinetic energy or to heating.
State that energy transferred depends on the appliance's power and how long it is on.
Recall and use energy transferred = power x time and energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference.
Explain how a device's power relates to potential difference, current and energy transferred in a given time.
Describe with examples how appliance power ratings relate to changes in stored energy.
Describe the National Grid as cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
Explain that step-up transformers raise potential difference for transmission and step-down transformers lower it for homes.
Explain why the National Grid is an efficient way to transfer energy.
Describe how rubbing insulating materials moves electrons from one to the other, leaving equal and opposite charges.
State that like charges repel and unlike charges attract, and that this is a non-contact force.
Describe static electricity and sparking produced by rubbing surfaces.
Describe evidence that charged objects exert forces without touching.
Explain static phenomena in terms of electron transfer.
State that a charged object has an electric field that is strongest close to it and weakens with distance.
State that a charge in the field feels a force that grows as distance shrinks.
Draw the electric field pattern of an isolated charged sphere.
Explain the electric field concept and how it accounts for non-contact forces and sparking.

topics.title: 4.3.1 Changes of state and the particle model

outcomes.text: Recall and use density = mass / volume, including changes where mass is conserved.
Use the particle model to explain the states of matter and differences in density.
Draw simple diagrams showing the particle arrangement in solids, liquids and gases.
Explain density differences between states using the arrangement of particles.
Required practical 5: measure the density of regular and irregular solids and liquids, using displacement for irregular shapes.
Describe how mass is conserved when substances melt, freeze, boil, evaporate, condense or sublimate.
Explain that changes of state are physical, because the material recovers its properties when reversed.
Define internal energy as the total kinetic and potential energy of all particles in a system.
Explain that heating raises particle energy, which either raises temperature or changes state.

subtopics.title: Temperature change and specific heat capacity

outcomes.text: State that a temperature rise depends on mass, material and energy input.
Use change in thermal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change.
State what specific heat capacity means.
State that latent heat is the energy for a change of state, which alters internal energy but not temperature.
Define specific latent heat as the energy to change the state of 1 kg with no temperature change.
Use energy for a change of state = mass x specific latent heat.
Distinguish latent heat of fusion from latent heat of vaporisation.
Interpret heating and cooling graphs that include changes of state.
Distinguish specific heat capacity from specific latent heat.
State that gas molecules move randomly and that temperature relates to their average kinetic energy.
State that changing the temperature of a gas at constant volume changes its pressure.
Explain how molecular motion relates to a gas's temperature and pressure.
Explain qualitatively how gas temperature and pressure are related at constant volume.
Describe how gas pressure produces a net force at right angles to container walls.
Explain with particles why a larger volume at constant temperature lowers pressure.
Use pressure x volume = constant to find pressure or volume changes of a fixed mass of gas.
(Higher tier) State that work is energy transfer by a force and that work on a gas raises its internal energy and maybe temperature.
(Higher tier) Explain why a bicycle pump warms up when compressing air.
State that atoms have a radius of about 1 x 10 to the minus 10 metres.
Describe an atom as a positive nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons.
State that the nucleus is under 1/10 000 of the atom's radius yet holds most of its mass.
Explain that electrons move between energy levels by absorbing or emitting electromagnetic radiation.
Recognise expressions given in standard form.

subtopics.title: Atomic number, mass number and isotopes

outcomes.text: State that atoms are neutral because electrons equal protons.
Define atomic number as the number of protons and mass number as protons plus neutrons.
Explain that isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.
State that atoms become positive ions by losing outer electrons.
Relate differences between isotopes to how their identities, charges and masses are written.
Explain that new evidence can lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
Describe the early indivisible-sphere model and the plum pudding model.
Describe how alpha scattering showed a charged nucleus holding the atom's mass, replacing the plum pudding model.
Describe Bohr's adaptation with electrons orbiting at set distances.
Describe the discovery of the proton and Chadwick's evidence for neutrons.
Explain why scattering evidence changed the atomic model and compare plum pudding with the nuclear model.
Explain that unstable nuclei emit radiation in a random process called radioactive decay.
Define activity (measured in becquerels) and count rate.
Describe alpha, beta, gamma and neutron emissions and what each is.
Compare alpha, beta and gamma by penetration, range in air and ionising power.
Apply knowledge of radiation to its uses and evaluate the best source for a situation.
Use symbols for alpha and beta particles in nuclear equations.
Explain how alpha, beta and gamma emission change the mass and charge of a nucleus.
Write balanced equations for single alpha and beta decay by balancing atomic and mass numbers.
State that radioactive decay is random.
Define half-life as the time for the number of nuclei, or the count rate or activity, to halve.
Explain half-life and how it relates to the random nature of decay.
Determine the half-life of an isotope from given data.
(Higher tier) Calculate the net decline as a ratio after a number of half-lives.
Define radioactive contamination and say the hazard comes from decay of the contaminating atoms.
Define irradiation and state that the irradiated object does not become radioactive.
Compare the hazards of contamination and irradiation.
Describe precautions needed against hazards from radioactive sources.
Explain why studies of radiation's effects on humans are published for peer review.

topics.title: 4.4.3 Hazards and uses of radioactive emissions and of background radiation (physics only)

outcomes.text: Name natural sources of background radiation, such as rocks and cosmic rays, and man-made sources, such as fallout.
State that background level and dose depend on occupation and location.
State that radiation dose is measured in sieverts, with 1000 millisieverts in one sievert.
State that radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-lives.
Explain why the hazard of a radioactive material depends on its half-life.
State that radiation is used in medicine to explore internal organs and to control or destroy unwanted tissue.
Describe and evaluate these medical uses of radiation.
Evaluate perceived risks of nuclear radiation using given data and consequences.
Define nuclear fission as the splitting of a large unstable nucleus such as uranium or plutonium.
State that fission usually needs the nucleus to absorb a neutron first.
Describe the split into two smaller nuclei with two or three neutrons and gamma rays emitted, releasing energy.
Explain how neutrons start a chain reaction, controlled in reactors and uncontrolled in weapons.
Draw and interpret diagrams of fission and a chain reaction.
Define nuclear fusion as light nuclei joining to form a heavier one, converting some mass to radiation energy.
Distinguish scalar quantities, which have magnitude only, from vectors, which also have direction.
Represent a vector by an arrow whose length shows magnitude and whose direction shows direction.
Define a force as a push or pull from an interaction with another object.
Distinguish contact forces from non-contact forces and give examples of each.
State that force is a vector.
Describe the interaction of pairs of objects producing a force on each, shown as vectors.
Define weight as the force of gravity on an object, caused by a gravitational field.
State that weight depends on the local gravitational field strength.
Recall and use weight = mass x gravitational field strength.
State that weight acts at the centre of mass and is directly proportional to mass.
State that weight is measured with a calibrated spring balance (newtonmeter).
Define a resultant force as the single force with the same effect as several forces.
Calculate the resultant of two forces acting in a straight line.
(Higher tier) Describe forces on an isolated object and use free body diagrams, including balanced forces.
(Higher tier) Explain how a force can be resolved into two components at right angles.
(Higher tier) Use scale vector diagrams to resolve forces, show equilibrium and find a resultant's size and direction.
Explain that work is done when a force moves an object through a distance.
Recall and use work done = force x distance moved along the line of action.
State that one joule is one newton-metre and convert between them.
Describe the energy transfer when work is done.
Explain that work against friction raises an object's temperature.
Give examples of forces involved in stretching, bending or compressing an object.
Explain why changing a stationary object's shape needs more than one force.
Describe elastic versus inelastic deformation.
State that extension is proportional to force below the limit of proportionality.
Recall and use force = spring constant x extension, including compression.
Explain that work done stretching a spring is stored as elastic potential energy if not inelastically deformed.
Distinguish linear from non-linear force-extension relationships.
Calculate a spring constant in linear cases.
Interpret data from a force-extension investigation.
Calculate work done stretching a spring using 0.5 x spring constant x extension squared.
Calculate stored energy values and energy transfers.
Required practical 6: investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring.
Describe examples where forces cause rotation.
Define the moment of a force and use moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot.
State that a balanced object has equal clockwise and anticlockwise moments.
Calculate a force or distance for a balanced object.
Explain how simple levers and gears transmit rotational effects of forces.

topics.title: 4.5.5 Pressure and pressure differences in fluids (physics only)

outcomes.text: State that a fluid is a liquid or a gas and that its pressure acts at right angles to any surface.
Recall and use pressure = force / area.

subtopics.title: Pressure in a liquid column and upthrust

outcomes.text: (Higher tier) Use pressure = height x density x gravitational field strength for a liquid column.
(Higher tier) Explain why pressure in a liquid rises with depth and density.
(Higher tier) Calculate pressure differences at different depths.
(Higher tier) Explain upthrust as the upward resultant force from greater pressure on the bottom of a submerged object.
(Higher tier) Describe factors influencing floating and sinking.
Describe the atmosphere as a thin layer of air that thins with altitude.
Explain that air molecules colliding with a surface create atmospheric pressure.
Explain why atmospheric pressure falls with height because less air lies above.
Define distance as a scalar and displacement as a vector measured in a straight line from start to finish.
Express a displacement as magnitude and direction.
State that speed is a scalar and that it is rarely constant.
Recall typical speeds: walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s, and sound in air 330 m/s.
Recall typical speeds for transport and note that wind and sound speeds vary.
Measure distance and time to calculate speed.
Recall and use distance = speed x time for constant speed.
Calculate average speed for non-uniform motion.
Define velocity as speed in a given direction and a vector.
Explain the scalar-vector distinction for displacement, distance, velocity and speed.
(Higher tier) Explain that circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity.
Represent motion along a line with a distance-time graph.
Calculate speed from the gradient of a distance-time graph.
(Higher tier) Find speed at an instant for accelerating motion using a tangent.
Draw and interpret distance-time graphs, moving between graphical and numerical form.
Recall and use acceleration = change in velocity / time taken.
State that a slowing object is decelerating.
Estimate the size of everyday accelerations.
Calculate acceleration from the gradient of a velocity-time graph.
(Higher tier) Find distance travelled from the area under a velocity-time graph, including by counting squares.
Draw and interpret velocity-time graphs.
Use v squared minus u squared = 2 x acceleration x distance for uniform acceleration.
State that free fall near Earth has acceleration of about 9.8 m/s squared.
Explain that an object falling through a fluid accelerates until resultant force is zero and it reaches terminal velocity.
(Physics only) Draw and interpret velocity-time graphs for terminal velocity and explain them using forces.
State that with zero resultant force a stationary object stays still and a moving one keeps constant velocity.
Explain that at steady speed resistive forces balance the driving force.
State that velocity changes only if a resultant force acts.
Apply the first law to uniform motion and to changes in speed or direction.
(Higher tier) Define inertia as the tendency to stay at rest or in uniform motion.
State that acceleration is proportional to resultant force and inversely proportional to mass.
Recall and use resultant force = mass x acceleration.
(Higher tier) Explain that inertial mass measures how hard it is to change velocity, defined as force over acceleration.
Estimate speeds, accelerations and forces in large accelerations of road transport.
Required practical 7: investigate how force and mass each affect acceleration.
State that two interacting objects exert equal and opposite forces on each other.
Apply the third law to equilibrium situations.
Define stopping distance as thinking distance plus braking distance.
State that for a given braking force a greater speed gives a longer stopping distance.
(Physics only) Estimate emergency stopping distances over typical speeds.
(Physics only) Interpret graphs of speed against stopping distance.
State that reaction times vary, typically 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
Explain how tiredness, drugs, alcohol and distractions affect reaction time.
Explain methods of measuring reaction time and recall typical results.
Interpret and evaluate simple measurements of students' reaction times.
Evaluate how factors affect thinking distance from data.
Describe how wet or icy roads and poor brakes or tyres increase braking distance.
Explain factors affecting emergency stopping distance and the safety implications.
Estimate how stopping distance changes across typical speeds.
Explain that friction in braking reduces kinetic energy and heats the brakes.
State that higher speed needs greater braking force to stop in a given distance.
State that a greater braking force gives greater deceleration, risking overheated brakes or loss of control.
Explain the dangers of large decelerations.
(Higher tier) Estimate forces in the deceleration of road vehicles.
Recall and use momentum = mass x velocity.
State that in a closed system total momentum before an event equals total momentum after.
Describe and explain momentum in events such as collisions.
(Physics only) Carry out calculations for events such as two-object collisions.
(Physics only) State that a force on a moving object changes its momentum.
(Physics only) Use force = change in momentum / time, combining F = ma and acceleration = change in velocity / time.
(Physics only) Explain airbags, seat belts, crash mats, helmets and cushioned surfaces through rate of change of momentum.
(Physics only) Apply the equations relating force, mass, velocity and acceleration.

topics.title: 4.6.1 Waves in air, fluids and solids

outcomes.text: State that waves are transverse or longitudinal, with water ripples transverse.
Describe longitudinal waves as having compressions and rarefactions, as with sound in air.
Describe the difference between longitudinal and transverse waves.
Describe evidence that ripples and sound transfer the wave, not the water or air.
Describe waves using amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period.
Define amplitude, wavelength and frequency.
Use period = 1 / frequency.
State that wave speed is the speed at which energy moves through the medium.
Recall and use wave speed = frequency x wavelength.
Identify amplitude and wavelength from diagrams.
Describe a method to measure the speed of sound in air.
Describe a method to measure the speed of ripples on water.
(Physics only) Relate changes in velocity, frequency and wavelength when sound passes between media.
Required practical 8: choose suitable apparatus to measure frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and in a solid.
State that waves can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted at the boundary between two materials.
Construct ray diagrams showing reflection of a wave at a surface.
Describe the effects of reflection, transmission and absorption at material interfaces.
Required practical 9 (physics only): investigate reflection of light by different surfaces and refraction by different substances.
(Higher tier, physics only) State that sound travelling through solids makes them vibrate, and the ear drum vibrates to give hearing.
(Higher tier, physics only) Describe processes converting sound waves to vibrations in solids and back.
(Higher tier, physics only) Explain why such conversion works only over a limited frequency range, limiting human hearing.
(Higher tier, physics only) Recall the normal human hearing range of 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
(Higher tier, physics only) Explain how differences in velocity, absorption and reflection of waves reveal hidden structures.
(Higher tier, physics only) Describe ultrasound as above human hearing, partly reflected at boundaries, with echo time giving distance, for medical and industrial imaging.
(Higher tier, physics only) Describe seismic P-waves as longitudinal and S-waves as transverse, with S-waves unable to pass through liquid.
(Higher tier, physics only) Explain how P-waves and S-waves give evidence for the size and structure of the Earth's core.
(Higher tier, physics only) Describe echo sounding for detecting objects and measuring water depth.
(Higher tier, physics only) Recognise that seismic study gave new evidence about parts of the Earth we cannot observe.
State that electromagnetic waves are transverse and transfer energy from a source to an absorber.
State that they form a continuous spectrum and all travel at the same speed in a vacuum or air.
Order the groups from long wavelength to short: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
State that eyes detect only visible light, a limited part of the spectrum.
Give examples showing energy transfer by electromagnetic waves.

subtopics.title: Reflection, refraction and absorption of EM waves

outcomes.text: (Higher tier) Explain that substances absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves differently by wavelength.
(Higher tier) Explain that refraction comes from different wave speeds in different substances.
Construct ray diagrams showing refraction at a boundary between two media.
(Higher tier) Use wave front diagrams to explain refraction by the change of speed between media.
Required practical 10: investigate how a surface's nature affects infrared radiation absorbed or radiated.

subtopics.title: Generation, absorption and hazards of EM waves

outcomes.text: (Higher tier) State that oscillations in electrical circuits produce radio waves.
(Higher tier) Explain that absorbed radio waves can induce an alternating current of the same frequency.
State that atomic and nuclear changes generate or absorb electromagnetic waves, and gamma rays come from the nucleus.
State that ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays can harm body tissue depending on type and dose.
Define radiation dose as a measure of risk of harm, in sieverts.
Draw conclusions from data about the risks and consequences of radiation exposure.
State that ultraviolet can age skin and cause skin cancer, and X-rays and gamma rays can cause gene mutation and cancer.
Give uses: radio waves for broadcasting, microwaves for satellites and cooking, infrared for heaters, cooking and cameras.
Give uses: visible light for fibre optics, ultraviolet for efficient lamps and tanning, X-rays and gamma rays for medical imaging and treatment.
(Higher tier) Explain briefly why each type of wave suits its application.
Explain that a lens forms an image by refracting light and that a convex lens brings parallel rays to a principal focus.
Define focal length as the distance from the lens to the principal focus.
State that a convex lens makes real or virtual images and a concave lens always virtual ones.
Construct ray diagrams showing similarities and differences between convex and concave lenses.
Use magnification = image height / object height, a unitless ratio.
Investigate the magnification produced by a range of convex lenses.
State that each colour of visible light has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency.
Distinguish specular reflection from smooth surfaces and diffuse reflection from rough surfaces.
Explain that colour filters absorb some wavelengths and transmit others.
Explain that an opaque object's colour depends on which wavelengths it reflects strongly.
State that objects reflecting all wavelengths look white and those absorbing all look black.
Distinguish transparent from translucent objects.
Explain how colour relates to absorption, transmission and reflection, and the effect of filters.
State that all bodies emit and absorb infrared radiation and hotter bodies radiate more in a given time.
Define a perfect black body as absorbing all incident radiation, so it is the best possible emitter.
Explain that all bodies emit radiation whose intensity and wavelength spread depend on temperature.
(Higher tier) Explain that a body at constant temperature absorbs and emits at equal rates and warms when absorbing faster.
(Higher tier) State the factors setting the Earth's temperature, including absorption, emission and reflection into space.
(Higher tier) Explain a body's temperature using the balance of absorbed and emitted radiation with everyday examples.
(Higher tier) Use or draw diagrams showing how radiation affects the Earth's surface and atmosphere temperature.

topics.title: 4.7.1 Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic forces and fields

outcomes.text: State that poles are where magnetic forces are strongest, like poles repel and unlike poles attract, as non-contact forces.
Distinguish permanent magnets from induced magnets, which are always attracted and quickly lose magnetism.
Describe attraction and repulsion between permanent magnet poles and the difference between permanent and induced magnets.
Define the magnetic field as the region where a magnet or magnetic material (iron, steel, cobalt, nickel) feels a force.
State that the force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always attractive.
State that field strength falls with distance and is greatest at the poles.
State that field direction is that of the force on a north pole, running from north to south pole outside the magnet.
Describe the compass as a small magnet pointing along the Earth's field.
Describe how to plot a magnet's field pattern with a compass.
Draw the field pattern of a bar magnet showing how strength and direction change.
Explain how compass behaviour is evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic.
State that a current in a wire produces a magnetic field depending on current and distance.
Explain that a solenoid strengthens the field, which is strong and uniform inside it.
State that a solenoid's field resembles a bar magnet's and an iron core strengthens it to make an electromagnet.
Describe how the magnetic effect of a current can be demonstrated.
Draw field patterns for a straight current-carrying wire and a solenoid, with direction.
Explain how a solenoid increases the magnetic effect of a current.
(Physics only) Interpret diagrams of electromagnetic devices to explain how they work.

subtopics.title: Fleming's left-hand rule and force on a conductor

outcomes.text: (Higher tier) Define the motor effect as the force between a current-carrying conductor and a magnet.
(Higher tier) Show how Fleming's left-hand rule relates force, current and field directions.
(Higher tier) Recall the factors that affect the force on the conductor.
(Higher tier) Use force = magnetic flux density x current x length for a conductor at right angles to the field.
(Higher tier) State that a coil carrying current in a magnetic field tends to rotate, the basis of a motor.
(Higher tier) Explain how the force on a conductor turns the coil in an electric motor.
(Higher tier, physics only) State that loudspeakers and headphones use the motor effect to turn current variations into sound pressure variations.
(Higher tier, physics only) Explain how a moving-coil loudspeaker and headphones work.

topics.title: 4.7.3 Induced potential, transformers and the National Grid (physics only, higher tier)

outcomes.text: Explain that a conductor moving relative to a field, or a changing field, induces a potential difference, and a current in a complete circuit: the generator effect.
State that the induced current's field opposes the original change.
Recall the factors affecting the size of the induced potential difference or current.
Recall the factors affecting its direction.
Apply the generator effect principles in a given context.
State that an alternator generates ac and a dynamo generates dc using the generator effect.
Explain how alternators and dynamos work.
Draw and interpret graphs of generated potential difference against time.
State that microphones use the generator effect to turn sound pressure variations into current variations.
Explain how a moving-coil microphone works.
Describe a basic transformer with primary and secondary coils on an iron core, iron being easily magnetised.
Use the ratio Vp / Vs = np / ns for the turns on each coil.
Distinguish step-up transformers (Vs greater than Vp) from step-down (Vs less than Vp).
State that a 100% efficient transformer has output power equal to input power: Vs x Is = Vp x Ip.
Explain how an alternating current in one coil induces a current in another.
Explain how the potential difference ratio depends on the turns ratio.
Calculate the current drawn from the input to give a particular power output.
Relate transformer equations to the advantages of high-potential-difference transmission.

topics.title: 4.8.1 Solar system; stability of orbital motions; satellites

outcomes.text: Describe the solar system: the Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets and moons as natural satellites.
State that the solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.
State that the Sun formed from a dust and gas nebula pulled together by gravity.
Explain how gravity drawing dust and gas together starts fusion reactions in a star.
Explain that fusion balances gravitational collapse against expansion, giving equilibrium.
State that a star's life cycle depends on its size.
Describe the life cycle of a star the size of the Sun and of a much more massive star.
State that stellar fusion makes all natural elements, those heavier than iron forming in a supernova.
Explain how fusion leads to the formation of new elements.
State that gravity provides the force that keeps planets and satellites in circular orbits.
Describe similarities and differences between planets, moons and artificial satellites.
(Higher tier) Explain that in circular orbit gravity changes velocity but not speed.
(Higher tier) Explain that a stable orbit's radius must change if speed changes.
Describe the increase in wavelength of light from distant galaxies, bigger for faster, further galaxies: red-shift.
State that red-shift is evidence that the universe is expanding and supports the Big Bang theory.
Describe the Big Bang theory as starting from a very small, extremely hot and dense region.
State that supernova observations since 1998 suggest distant galaxies recede ever faster.
Explain qualitatively the red-shift from receding galaxies.
Explain that speed changing with distance is evidence of expansion.
Explain how red-shift supports the Big Bang model.
Explain how scientists use observations to reach theories such as the Big Bang.
Recognise that much remains unexplained, such as dark mass and dark energy.
